name: Adobe
lede: Adobe is the color of sun-dried clay brick, a muted reddish orange-brown; the name is probably borrowed from the brick itself.

sections.title: A brick's name
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines adobe as a pinkish red, probably named for the sun-baked clay bricks of Latin America that share the word, and also gives the form adobe red [1]. The word "probably" is Paterson's own, and the books read do not trace the name any further [1].

The color is not the same as a software company's name or the Adobe RGB color space, a wide-gamut standard from 1998 that Westland describes in his entries on gamuts and RGB [2]. The two share a word, nothing else.

sections.title: On the old charts
sections.body:
The library finds the color in four systems: Ridgway's 1912 atlas (plate XIV), the 1955 ISCC-NBS blocks, the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, which dates the name to 1922, and the xkcd survey [3]. Ridgway's near-twin is Cinnamon-Rufous, only 1.7 units away [3]. Its nearest everyday name is [[terracotta]], about nine units away [3].

On screens the swatch is a clay orange; Paterson calls adobe a "pinkish red", rosier than this swatch [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch color is more common in museum paintings than most named colors: 310 of 23,781 paintings contain it, about 1.3 per cent [4]. It is over-represented in Raphael, in 5 of 36 paintings, and in Modigliani, in 4 of 18, and in Indian painting, in 41 of 721, especially the Pahari school, 11 of 118 [4]. Skin and brick-red earth pigments are the likely reasons, but our data cannot say; it only shows photographed color, not pigment [4].

questions.q: What is the color probably named after, per Paterson?
True or false: the color is named after the Adobe RGB color space.

openers: The color named for sun-dried brick shows up in 1.3 per cent of the paintings in our archive.
